title: Counting and numbers
subject: Mathematics
summary: Counting means matching one number word to each object in a group. The last number you say tells you how many objects there are.
points: Numbers go 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on; each number is one more than the one before it.
We compare groups using more than, less than, or equal to.
Numbers can be shown as numerals (7), words (seven) or objects (seven dots).
example: Count the apples: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. There are 5 apples. If you eat one, 4 are left.
mistakes: Saying the number too fast and skipping an object.
Forgetting that zero means none, not one.

title: Addition and subtraction
subject: Mathematics
summary: Addition puts groups together to find a total; subtraction takes one number away from another to find what is left or the difference.
points: The + sign means add and the − sign means subtract.
Addition and subtraction undo each other: 5 + 3 = 8, so 8 − 3 = 5.
When adding two-digit numbers, add the ones first, then the tens.
example: 24 + 13: ones 4 + 3 = 7, tens 2 + 1 = 3, so the answer is 37.
mistakes: Forgetting to carry a ten when the ones add to more than 9.
Subtracting the smaller digit from the larger one instead of borrowing.

title: Multiplication and tables
subject: Mathematics
summary: Multiplication is repeated addition of the same number: 4 × 3 means 4 added three times.
points: Multiplication tables up to 10 make bigger sums quick.
4 × 3 and 3 × 4 give the same answer, so order does not change a product.
An array of rows and columns is a picture of multiplication.
example: 5 × 6 = 30, which is the same as 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5.
mistakes: Mixing up a table row, such as 7 × 8 with 7 × 9.
Adding instead of multiplying when the question says times.

title: Division
subject: Mathematics
summary: Division splits a number into equal groups or shares. It is the inverse of multiplication.
points: 12 ÷ 3 asks how many groups of 3 fit into 12.
The number left over when groups cannot be equal is the remainder.
Every division can be checked with multiplication: quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend.
example: 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2, because 3 × 5 = 15 and 17 − 15 = 2.
mistakes: Writing the remainder as a decimal when the question asks for a whole-number remainder.
Dividing the divisor by the dividend instead.

title: Place value
subject: Mathematics
summary: Place value tells what a digit is worth depending on its position: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands and beyond.
points: In 4,582 the 5 is worth 500 because it sits in the hundreds place.
Expanded form shows the parts: 4,582 = 4,000 + 500 + 80 + 2.
To compare large numbers, compare the digits from the left.
example: In 7,306 the digit 3 is in the hundreds place, so its value is 300.
aliases: numbers from twenty one to fifty
mistakes: Confusing face value (the digit itself) with place value (what it is worth).

title: Fractions
subject: Mathematics
summary: A fraction shows equal parts of a whole. The denominator says how many equal parts there are and the numerator says how many you have.
points: In 3/4 the whole is cut into 4 equal parts and 3 are taken.
Equivalent fractions look different but name the same amount: 1/2 = 2/4.
Fractions with the same denominator can be added by adding the numerators.
example: 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4. The denominator stays 4 because the size of the parts has not changed.
mistakes: Adding the denominators as well as the numerators.
Thinking 1/8 is bigger than 1/4 because 8 is bigger than 4.

title: Decimals
subject: Mathematics
summary: Decimals write fractions whose denominators are 10, 100 or 1000 using a decimal point.
points: The first place after the point is tenths, the next is hundredths.
0.5 is the same as 1/2 and 0.25 is the same as 1/4.
Line up the decimal points before adding or subtracting.
mistakes: Writing 2.4 + 1.25 as 2.4 + 1.25 = 2.65 by misaligning the places.

title: Shapes and patterns
subject: Mathematics
summary: Shapes have names based on their sides and corners, and patterns repeat in a rule you can continue.
points: A triangle has 3 sides, a square and rectangle have 4, a pentagon has 5.
A cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone and sphere are solid shapes.
A pattern has a rule such as add 2, or repeat red, blue, red, blue.
example: 2, 4, 6, 8, … follows the rule add 2, so the next number is 10.
aliases: what is long what is round
mistakes: Calling every four-sided shape a square; a square needs equal sides and right angles.

title: Measurement
subject: Mathematics
summary: Measurement compares an object with a standard unit of length, mass or capacity.
points: Length uses millimetres, centimetres, metres and kilometres.
Mass uses grams and kilograms; capacity uses millilitres and litres.
example: A 2.5 m rope is 250 cm long, because 2.5 × 100 = 250.
mistakes: Multiplying when changing from a smaller unit to a larger one.

title: Time and calendar
subject: Mathematics
summary: Time is read on a clock in hours and minutes, and the calendar arranges days into weeks and months.
points: 1 hour = 60 minutes and 1 minute = 60 seconds.
The short hand shows hours and the long hand shows minutes.
A year has 12 months and 365 days, or 366 in a leap year.
example: A film starts at 4:45 and runs 1 hour 30 minutes, so it ends at 6:15.
mistakes: Treating 1 hour 30 minutes as 1.30 hours; it is 1.5 hours.

title: Money
subject: Mathematics
summary: Money is counted in rupees and paise, and bills are added and subtracted like decimals.
points: ₹1 = 100 paise.
Write amounts with two decimal places, such as ₹45.50.
Change is the amount paid minus the total cost.
example: A notebook costs ₹32.50 and you pay ₹50, so the change is ₹17.50.
mistakes: Forgetting to convert paise to rupees before adding amounts.

title: Perimeter and area
subject: Mathematics
summary: Perimeter is the distance around a shape; area is the space inside it.
points: Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 × (length + breadth).
Area of a rectangle = length × breadth; area of a square = side × side.
Area is measured in square units such as cm².
example: A rectangle is 8 cm by 5 cm: perimeter 2 × (8 + 5) = 26 cm, area 8 × 5 = 40 cm².
mistakes: Writing area in cm instead of cm².
Using the area formula for perimeter.

title: Factors and multiples
subject: Mathematics
summary: A factor divides a number exactly with no remainder; a multiple is what you get when you multiply that number by a whole number.
points: Factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
Multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16 and so on.
A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
example: 12 is a multiple of both 3 and 4, and both 3 and 4 are factors of 12.
aliases: be my multiple i will be your factor
mistakes: Mixing up factors and multiples.
Calling 1 a prime number; it has only one factor.

title: Data handling
subject: Mathematics
summary: Data handling collects information and shows it in tables, pictographs and bar graphs so it is easy to compare.
points: Tally marks group counts in fives.
A pictograph uses a symbol, and a key says what one symbol stands for.
A bar graph uses bars of equal width whose heights show the numbers.
example: If one symbol means 5 students, then 4 symbols mean 20 students.
mistakes: Reading the bar height as the count when the axis uses a scale of 2 or 5.

title: Percentage
subject: Mathematics
summary: Percent means per hundred, so 25% is 25 out of every 100.
points: 50% is half, 25% is a quarter and 10% is one tenth.
To find a percentage of a number, divide by 100 and multiply.
Percentages compare quantities of different sizes fairly.
mistakes: Finding 20% by dividing by 20 instead of multiplying by 20/100.

title: Average
subject: Mathematics
summary: The average, or mean, shares a total equally among all the items.
points: Average = total of all values ÷ number of values.
The average lies between the smallest and largest values.
Averages hide how spread out the values are.

formulas.name: Mean
formulas.expr: mean = sum of values ÷ number of values

example: Marks 60, 70 and 80 give an average of (60 + 70 + 80) ÷ 3 = 70.
mistakes: Dividing by the highest value instead of by how many values there are.

title: Alphabet, vowels and phonics
subject: English
summary: English has 26 letters. Five are vowels (a, e, i, o, u) and the rest are consonants, and their sounds build words.
points: Letters have capital and small forms: A a, B b.
A vowel sound can be short as in cat or long as in cake.
Blending sounds such as c-a-t builds the word cat.
example: b + a + t says bat; add s and you get bats.
mistakes: Treating y as always a consonant; it acts as a vowel in words like sky.

title: Nouns and pronouns
subject: English
summary: A noun names a person, place, animal or thing. A pronoun replaces a noun so it does not have to repeat.
points: Common nouns name general things (city); proper nouns name particular ones (Delhi) and take a capital letter.
Singular means one and plural means more than one.
Pronouns include I, you, he, she, it, we and they.
example: Riya lost Riya's bag becomes Riya lost her bag, using the pronoun her.
mistakes: Using he for a thing instead of it.
Writing proper nouns without capital letters.

title: Verbs and tenses
subject: English
summary: A verb shows action or state, and tense tells when it happens: past, present or future.
points: Simple present: I walk. Simple past: I walked. Simple future: I will walk.
Adding -s to a present-tense verb for he, she or it: she walks.
Irregular verbs change form: go, went, gone.
example: They play today, they played yesterday, and they will play tomorrow.
mistakes: Using the past form after did: did went instead of did go.

title: Adjectives and adverbs
subject: English
summary: Adjectives describe nouns and adverbs describe verbs, adjectives or other adverbs.
points: Adjectives answer what kind, which one or how many: a tall tree.
Adverbs often answer how, when or where and many end in -ly: she ran quickly.
Comparing uses -er/-est or more/most: taller, tallest.
example: The quiet boy read silently: quiet describes the boy, silently describes how he read.
mistakes: Writing gooder instead of better.

title: Sentences and punctuation
subject: English
summary: A sentence expresses a complete idea and begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark.
points: A statement ends with a full stop, a question with a question mark and a strong feeling with an exclamation mark.
Commas separate items in a list and mark pauses.
A sentence needs a subject and a verb: Birds fly.
example: Where is my bag? It ends with a question mark because it asks something.
mistakes: Joining two complete sentences with only a comma.
Forgetting the capital letter at the start.

title: Paragraph and letter writing
subject: English
summary: A paragraph develops one main idea in a group of sentences, and a letter has a greeting, a body and a closing.
points: Start a paragraph with a topic sentence and support it with details.
An informal letter is friendly; a formal letter is polite and brief.
Use linking words such as first, then, because and finally.
example: Topic sentence: Trees help us in many ways. Details follow about shade, fruit and clean air.
mistakes: Putting several unrelated ideas in the same paragraph.
Leaving out the date or closing in a formal letter.

title: Reading comprehension
subject: English
summary: Comprehension answers questions about a passage using evidence from the text.
points: Read the questions first, then the passage, so you know what to look for.
Answer in your own words but stay close to the passage.
A 'why' question usually needs a reason found in the text.
example: If the passage says the crow dropped stones into the pot to raise the water, the answer to 'how did it reach the water?' is the stones, not 'it was clever'.
mistakes: Copying whole sentences when the question asks for a short answer.
Adding facts that are not in the passage.

title: वर्णमाला और वर्ण
subject: Hindi
summary: हिंदी की वर्णमाला में स्वर (अ, आ, इ, ई आदि) और व्यंजन (क, ख, ग आदि) होते हैं; इनसे शब्द बनते हैं।
points: स्वर 11 (या 13) माने जाते हैं और व्यंजन 33 से 35 तक होते हैं।
व्यंजन के साथ स्वर की मात्रा जुड़ने से शब्द बनता है, जैसे क + ा = का।
अनुनासिक (चंद्रबिंदु) और अनुस्वार (बिंदु) उच्चारण बदलते हैं।
example: क + ि = कि, क + ी = की; दोनों का उच्चारण और अर्थ अलग होता है।
mistakes: 'ि' और 'ी' की मात्रा में भ्रम.
व्यंजन के नीचे लगने वाले रूप (जैसे क़) को भूल जाना।

title: संज्ञा, सर्वनाम और क्रिया
subject: Hindi
summary: संज्ञा किसी व्यक्ति, वस्तु, स्थान या भाव का नाम है; सर्वनाम संज्ञा की जगह आता है और क्रिया काम बताती है।
points: संज्ञा के भेद: व्यक्तिवाचक, जातिवाचक, भाववाचक।
सर्वनाम: मैं, तुम, वह, हम, वे आदि।
क्रिया का रूप कर्ता और काल के अनुसार बदलता है।
example: मोहन खेलता है — 'मोहन' संज्ञा है और 'खेलता है' क्रिया।
mistakes: भाववाचक संज्ञा (जैसे मिठास) को जातिवाचक समझना।

title: Living and non-living things
subject: Science
summary: Living things grow, need food, water and air, respond to their surroundings and reproduce; non-living things do not.
points: Living things breathe, grow and produce young ones.
Plants are living even though they do not move about.
A car moves and needs fuel, but it does not grow or reproduce, so it is non-living.
example: A seed grows into a plant and makes new seeds, so it is living; a stone does not change by itself.
mistakes: Deciding something is living only because it moves.

title: Plants and their parts
subject: Science
summary: A plant usually has roots, a stem, leaves, flowers and fruit, and each part does a particular job.
points: Roots hold the plant in the soil and absorb water and minerals.
The stem carries water and supports leaves and flowers.
Leaves make food using sunlight, water and carbon dioxide.
example: A carrot is a root we eat, spinach is a leaf, and an apple is a fruit.
aliases: a seed tells a farmer's story
mistakes: Thinking all roots are underground; some climbers have aerial roots.

title: Animals and habitats
subject: Science
summary: Animals live where they can find food, water and shelter; that place is their habitat.
points: Land animals, water animals and birds have bodies suited to their homes.
Some animals are herbivores, some carnivores and some omnivores.
Adaptations such as thick fur or gills help animals survive in their habitat.
example: A fish has gills to take oxygen from water and fins to swim; a camel stores fat in its hump for dry months.
mistakes: Thinking a habitat is only a house or nest; it is the whole surroundings.

title: Human body and sense organs
subject: Science
summary: The body has five sense organs — eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin — and systems that work together.
points: Eyes see, ears hear, the nose smells, the tongue tastes and the skin feels.
The heart pumps blood and the lungs take in air.
Bones give shape and support; muscles help us move.
example: You smell food with your nose, taste it with your tongue and feel its heat with your skin.
mistakes: Saying the tongue detects smell; the nose does.

title: Food and nutrition
subject: Science
summary: Food gives energy and materials for growth, and a balanced diet includes carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water.
points: Carbohydrates and fats give energy; proteins help growth and repair.
Vitamins and minerals protect the body from disease.
A balanced diet includes grains, pulses, vegetables, fruit and milk.
example: Rice gives energy, dal gives protein, and an orange gives vitamin C.
mistakes: Thinking eating a lot means eating well; variety matters more than quantity.

title: Water and air
subject: Science
summary: Water and air are natural resources that living things need, and both can be polluted by human activity.
points: Water exists as ice, liquid water and water vapour.
Air is a mixture; it contains nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Boiling and filtering are common ways to make water safer to drink.
example: Clothes dry because water changes into vapour, which is evaporation.
aliases: too much water too little water
mistakes: Calling water vapour smoke; it is an invisible gas.

title: Weather and seasons
subject: Science
summary: Weather is what the air is like today; seasons are longer periods with a similar pattern of weather.
points: Sunny, cloudy, rainy, windy and snowy describe weather.
India has summer, monsoon and winter seasons in most regions.
Weather changes day to day, while climate is the average over many years.
example: A day can be cloudy but not rainy; the monsoon season brings many rainy days.
mistakes: Using weather and climate as if they meant the same thing.

title: Food chains
subject: Science
summary: A food chain shows who eats whom, starting with a plant that makes its own food.
points: Plants are producers; animals that eat plants are primary consumers.
Arrows in a food chain point from the food to the eater.
Many food chains linked together form a food web.
example: Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, with arrows showing the flow of energy.
mistakes: Pointing the arrow from the eater to the food.

title: Health and hygiene
subject: Science
summary: Good health comes from clean habits, safe food and water, enough sleep and regular activity.
points: Wash hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet.
Brush teeth twice a day and bathe regularly.
Cover your mouth when coughing or sneezing to reduce spreading germs.
example: Handwashing with soap removes germs that cause diarrhoea and other infections.
mistakes: Rinsing hands with water only; soap is what lifts germs off.

title: Maps and directions
subject: Geography
summary: A map is a drawing of an area from above, and directions help you find places on it.
points: The four main directions are north, south, east and west.
A map key explains symbols, and the scale tells how distances shrink.
North is usually at the top of a map.
example: If 1 cm on the map means 1 km, then 3 cm means 3 km.
mistakes: Reading the scale backwards, as if the map distances were real distances.

title: Community helpers
subject: Social Studies
summary: Community helpers are people whose work keeps a neighbourhood safe, healthy and running.
points: Doctors and nurses treat illness; teachers help children learn.
Police keep order, and firefighters put out fires and rescue people.
Farmers grow food and sanitation workers keep the area clean.
example: When there is a fire, the firefighter's job is to put it out and help people escape.
mistakes: Thinking only famous jobs count; everyday services matter just as much.
